title: Biograd na Moru Travel Guide: Beaches & Where to Stay
metaDescription: Plan your trip to Biograd na Moru with factual advice on driving routes, neighborhoods, parking, and beaches. Ideal for families and road trippers.
intro:
Biograd na Moru is a coastal town in northern Dalmatia, situated on a small peninsula midway between Zadar and Šibenik. It serves as a practical base for families and boaters due to its large marinas, accessible pebble beaches backed by pine forests, and proximity to the Kornati Islands and Vrana Lake.

The town is highly seasonal, operating at full capacity from June to September. It suits travelers looking for a traditional Croatian beach holiday with straightforward logistics, rather than those seeking high-end luxury or intense nightlife. Its flat terrain and shaded promenades make it particularly convenient for visitors with young children or limited mobility.

quickFacts.label: Best months
quickFacts.value: June and September for warm sea and fewer crowds

quickFacts.label: Main beach type
quickFacts.value: Pebble and gravel, with natural pine shade

quickFacts.label: Price level
quickFacts.value: Average for Croatia; cheaper than Split or Dubrovnik

quickFacts.label: Old town walkability
quickFacts.value: Compact and fully walkable, mostly car-free

areas.name: Centre & Old Town (Poluotok)
areas.bestFor: Dining, boat trips, and harbor access
areas.parking: Paid street parking and large municipal lots; often full in July/August
areas.beach: 10-15 minute walk to Dražica or Bošana
areas.summary: The historic peninsula holds the main restaurants, cafes, and ferry port. It is active in the evening but lacks immediate beach access.

areas.name: Dražica & Soline (South)
areas.parking: Private hotel/apartment parking is essential; public spots are scarce
areas.beach: Immediate access to Dražica (pebble) and Soline (sand/pebble mix)
areas.summary: This southern stretch is defined by large hotels, campsites, and a shaded promenade. It offers the best beach facilities and immediate water access.

areas.name: Bošana (North)
areas.parking: Easier street parking than the center; most apartments have driveways
areas.beach: Immediate access to Bošana Beach (pebble, less shade)
areas.summary: A residential area north of the marina primarily offering private apartment rentals. The local beach lacks the pine shade of the south but is generally less crowded.

areas.name: Kumenat
areas.parking: Mostly private parking provided by accommodation
areas.beach: Immediate access to Kumenat Beach (small pebble cove)
areas.summary: Located two kilometers south of the center, this small residential settlement is removed from the town noise. It offers a quieter, more isolated coastal experience.

gettingThere.car: 760 km, 8-9 hours via A10 (Austria) and A1 (Croatia). Requires Austrian vignette, Tauern tunnel toll, Slovenian vignette, and Croatian tolls.
gettingThere.other: Direct seasonal flights to Zadar (ZAD), then a 30-minute bus or taxi.

gettingThere.car: 620 km, 6.5-7.5 hours via A2/A9 (Austria) and A1/A4 (Slovenia). Requires Austrian and Slovenian vignettes, plus Croatian tolls.
gettingThere.other: Direct seasonal flights to Zadar (ZAD) or direct FlixBus to Biograd.

gettingThere.car: 650 km, 6.5-7 hours via M7 (Hungary) and A4/A1 (Croatia). Requires Hungarian e-vignette and Croatian tolls.
gettingThere.other: Seasonal direct flights to Zadar (ZAD) or train to Zagreb with a bus connection.

gettingThere.car: 340 km, 4 hours via A2 (Slovenia) and A1 (Croatia). Requires Slovenian vignette and Croatian tolls.
gettingThere.other: Direct bus services run in the summer taking around 5-6 hours.

gettingThere.car: 950 km, 10-11 hours via Vienna and Maribor. Requires Czech, Austrian, and Slovenian vignettes, plus Croatian tolls.
gettingThere.other: Direct seasonal flights to Zadar (ZAD) via low-cost carriers.

gettingThere.car: 1050 km, 11-12 hours via Slovakia and Hungary. Requires Slovak and Hungarian vignettes, plus Croatian tolls.
gettingThere.other: Direct flights to Zadar (ZAD) via Ryanair, then local transit.

whenToGo: July and August are the peak summer months, featuring sea temperatures around 25°C to 27°C, all tourist facilities open, but high prices and crowded beaches. June and September offer a better balance, with sea temperatures holding at 22°C to 24°C, lower accommodation rates, and manageable crowd levels, though occasional rain is possible. From October to May, Biograd na Moru is largely dormant; most hotels, seasonal restaurants, and beach facilities close, making it suitable only for passing travelers or those seeking complete solitude.

faq.question: Is it worth visiting?
faq.answer: Yes, if you want a straightforward family beach holiday or a base for sailing. It lacks the extensive historical architecture of Zadar or Šibenik but makes up for it with accessible, pine-shaded beaches.

faq.question: How many days?
faq.answer: Three to five days is optimal for a beach holiday and exploring the immediate area. A full week allows time for boat trips to the Kornati Islands or driving to Krka National Park.

faq.question: Best beach?
faq.answer: Dražica Beach is the most popular due to its Blue Flag status, gentle pebble entry, and heavy pine shade. Soline Beach, located slightly further south, offers patches of sand which are popular with small children.

faq.question: Do I need a car?
faq.answer: You do not need a car if you stay in Biograd and only plan to walk to the local beaches. However, a vehicle is highly recommended for day trips to nearby national parks, Zadar, or Vrana Lake.

faq.question: Where to park?
faq.answer: Parking in the center is divided into paid zones and is strictly enforced in summer. It is highly advised to book accommodation that includes guaranteed private parking to avoid daily fees and the struggle to find a spot.

faq.question: Is it good for families?
faq.answer: Yes, it is one of the most family-friendly towns in northern Dalmatia. The flat terrain, extensive pedestrian promenades, shaded beaches, and the nearby Dalmaland amusement park cater directly to children.
